s: Forms the strong masculine accusative singular of adjectives
Used to form abstract nouns, usually from adjectives but also from verbs and other nouns, denoting quality or state; -ness
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-nassī.

s: suffix applied to nouns and adjectives to form verbs
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-inōn, from Proto-Germanic *-inōną. Compare Old Frisian -nia, Old Saxon -nōn, Old High German -inōn, Old Norse -na.
From Proto-Germanic *-nahtijaz. Cognate with Old Norse -nættr. Equivalent to niht + -e.

s: Used to form gerunds, a type of verbal nouns, from verbs.
y: Unknown. Possibly related to nōþ.

s: alternative form of -e, as used to form the first person singular present indicative of strong verbs and class I weak verbs
noun suffix used to form descriptive names from adjectives
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-uk, *-ik, from Proto-Germanic *-ukaz, *-ikaz. Akin to Old Saxon -ik-, Middle Low German -ken, Middle Dutch -kin. More at English -kin.

s: Used to form the past participle of class II weak verbs
Forms adjectives from nouns and class 2 weak past participles, indicating the possession of a thing or a quality.
y: From a merger of Proto-Germanic *-ōdaz (adjective suffix) (from Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂tos) and Proto-Germanic *-ōdaz (class 2 weak past participle).

s: Forms the first and third person singular preterite indicative and singular subjunctive indicative of class II weak verbs
y: From the merger of several Proto-Germanic inflections.

s: Used to form the second person singular preterite indicative of class II weak verbs
Forms the plural preterite indicative of class II weak verbs
Used to form adjectives (usually from verbs) denoting inclination or tendency toward (compare English -ative)
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-ul, *-il, from Proto-Germanic *-ulaz, *-ilaz.

s: Marks the plural preterite indicative of strong verbs.
alternative form of -en (suffix forming past participles)

y: From Proto-Germanic *-ar-. Akin to Old High German -ar.

s: Suffix variant found on masculine a-stem nouns
y: From Proto-Germanic *-raz. Akin to Old Saxon -or, Old High German -ur.

s: Forms the comparative degree of adverbs
alternative form of -erian: a frequentative suffix
Used to form superlative adjectives and adverbs
y: Inherited from Proto-West Germanic *-ōst, from Proto-Germanic *-ōstaz.
From Proto-Germanic *-utją.

s: used to form concrete nouns from verbs
huntian (“to hunt”) + -oþ → huntoþ (“hunting; catch, prey, booty”)
faran (“to travel, fare”) + -oþ → faroþ (“water in motion, stream; ocean, sea, waves”)
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-ōþu, from Proto-Germanic *-ōþuz.

s: Forms ordinal numbers from twēntigoþa (“20th”) to hundendleftigoþa (“110th”) (and possibly unattested *hundtwelftigoþa (“120th”))
y:
Perhaps from a Proto-West Germanic *tegunþ- (“decad”, akin to *tehun "ten") in phrases such as Proto-West Germanic *þriddjō tegunþ- (“the third decad”) which came to be used as ordinals, leading the initial ordinal + *-teg- to be reanalysed as a cardinal number suffixed with *tigiwi (> Old English -tiġ) and the remaining -anþ/-unþ as an ordinal suffix. This was then supplied with *-ō (> Old English -a) like the other ordinals, resulting in a -anþō or -unþō that regularly develops to -oþa.
Alternaitvely, a later analogical formation from seofoþa (“seventh”), eahtoþa (“eighth”), nigoþa (“ninth”), and teogoþa, alternative form of tēoþa (“tenth”), with the -o- of the root reanalysed as belonging to the suffix (etymologically -da, -ta, -þa).

s: Used to form the comparative degree of adjectives
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-iʀō, *-ōʀō, from Proto-Germanic *-izô or Proto-Germanic *-ōzô

s: Used to form the genitive plural of adjectives
hundred, a counting or tally of 100
y: Inherited from Proto-Germanic *-raþ (“tally, tale, reckoning”). Akin to Gothic 𐍂𐌰𐌸𐌾𐍉 (raþjō, “number, reckoning”), Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐍂𐌰𐌸𐌾𐌰𐌽 (garaþjan, “to count”), Old English rǣden (“accounting, reckoning; condition”).

s: masculine agent suffix, originally applied only to nouns
y: From Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz, possibly from Latin -ārius.

s: Marks the strong feminine genitive, dative, and instrumental singular of adjectives.
y: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

s: suffix appended to nouns to indicate office, ownership, guardianship, governance or dominion, equivalent to English -dom
a bishopric; the diocese of a bishop
y: From rīċe (“dominion, realm”).

s: suffix meaning full of or like (compare -ful, -ous)
y: From rōf (“number of soldiers, array; fierce”). Akin to Old Saxon rōf (“numerous, vigorous, strong”), Old High German ruob (“numerous”), ruoba (“a number, multitude”), Old English ġerēfa (“reeve, official”). More at English sheriff.

s: Used to form the nominative/accusative plural of z-stem nouns
noun suffix denoting condition or state
y: From rǣden (“condition, state”), from Proto-Germanic *raidīniz (“arrangement, ordinance, authority”).

s: Feminine noun suffix forming nouns from adjectives and verbs
cweþan (“to say, speak”) + -s → cwiss (“a saying”) (earlier cwiþs)
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-issju, *-ussju, from Proto-Germanic *-isjō, *-usjō.

s: Ða toforan monan upgonge þa cwomon þær Scorpiones þæt wyrmcyn swa hie ær gewunelice wæron toweard þæs wætersciepes.
Then before moonrise those vermin called scorpions came, as they were accustomed, toward the water source.
y: Inherited from Proto-West Germanic *-skapi, from Proto-Germanic *-skapiz.

s: verbal suffix added to adjectives, nouns, and (rarely) verb roots, generally causing i-mutation in the stem
hwīnan (“whistle”) + -sian → hwinsian (“to make a whistling or whizzing sound”)
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-isōn, from Proto-Germanic *-isōną.
From Proto-West Germanic *-siunī. Cognate with Old High German -siuni. Equivalent to sīen + -e, literally “with a certain sight.”

s: Forms feminine ō-stem nouns denoting a tool or instrument.
y: From Proto-Germanic *-snō (*-asnō, *-isnō, *-usnō), from Proto-Indo-European *-sneh₂.

s: Used to form the second person singular present indicative of strong verbs and certain Class I weak verbs
suffix found in many placenames denoting "place" or "place of"
Bristol; literally: the place by the bridge
place, area; provenance of, office of, jurisdiction of
a place of peace, sanctuary, refuge, asylum
a baptistry, place where one is baptized
y: From stōw (“place”), from Proto-Germanic *stōō (“place”), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂w- (“to set, place”), from *steh₂- (“to stand”). Akin to Old Norse -stó (“place of”), Old Frisian stō (“place”), Gothic 𐍃𐍄𐍉𐌾𐌰𐌽 (stōjan, “to judge, place”). Compare the similar usage in forming toponyms in the cognate Indo-Iranian suffix -stan. See also stow.
Equivalent to strenġ + -e.

s: characterized by some specific condition or quality; same as
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-sam, from Proto-Germanic *-samaz (“same as”). Akin to Old Frisian -sum, Old High German -sam, Old Norse -samr, Gothic -𐍃𐌰𐌼𐍃 (-sams), -𐍃𐌰𐌼𐌰 (-sama, “same as”), Old English sam (“whether, or”), Old English same (“same”).

s: a resident or inhabitant of (usually used with placenames)
y: From *sǣta (“inhabitant, dweller”). Akin to Old Saxon -sētio, Old High German -sāzo (German -saß), Old English sittan (“to sit”).

s: residents, dwellers: forms names of peoples and places
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-sātī, originally meaning "residents" or "dwellers." Cognate with Old High German -sāti. Ultimately related to sittan.

s: Alternative form of -de used to form the first and third person singular preterite indicative of certain class I weak verbs
reċċan (“to explain, argue”) + -te → rehte (“I/he/she/it explained, argued”)

y: Ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *tehun (“ten”); doublet of tīen (“ten”)

s: -ty (used to form numerals denoting multiples of ten)
y: From Proto-Germanic *tigiwiz, plural of *teguz (“group of ten”).
From tūn, from Proto-West Germanic *tūn, from Proto-Germanic *tūną, from Proto-Celtic *dūnom, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“to finish, come full circle”).

s: ending used to form abstract nouns from adjectives (compare Modern English -ness), normally causing i-mutation, and remaining even when preceded by a long syllable
y: From suppletive fusion of ō-stem feminine singular nominative ending -u and Proto-Germanic *-į̄ (“feminine abstract ending”). Akin to Gothic feminine abstracts in -𐌴𐌹 (-ei) (compare 𐌼𐌹𐌺𐌹𐌻𐌴𐌹 (mikilei, “greatness”); 𐌳𐌹𐌿𐍀𐌴𐌹 (diupei, “depth”)).

s: Used to form the first person singular present indicative of strong verbs and class I weak verbs
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-u, from Proto-Germanic *-ō. Apocope should have caused the loss of this ending after heavy stems, but the Anglian dialects generally retained it by analogy with short stems, or for its morphological significance. In West Saxon, this apocope led to replacement with the subjunctive singular -e, which was then extended to short stem verbs as well.

s: Used to form the nominative singular of short ō-stem nouns
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-u, from Proto-Germanic *-ō

s: Used to form the nominative and accusative singular of short u-stem nouns
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-u, from Proto-Germanic *-uz

s: Used to form the nominative and accusative plural of short a-stem and all ija-stem neuter nouns
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-u, from Proto-Germanic *-ō

s: Forms the strong nominative feminine singular and strong nominative/accusative neuter plural of adjectives

y: From Proto-West Germanic *-uk, from Proto-Germanic *-ukaz (diminutive suffix).

s: Used to form the dative plural of essentially all nouns
Used to form the strong and weak dative and instrumental plural of adjectives
Used to form the strong dative singular of masculine and neuter adjectives
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-um, possibly from Proto-Germanic *-amaz with reduction and analogical zero-grade, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *-mos, the dative-ablative plural ending. Cognate to modern German -en and Polish -om.

s: used to form the superlative of Old English adjectives
used in combination with other superlative endings
y: From Proto-Germanic *-umô.

s: alternative form of -on (strong plural past indicative suffix)
forming nouns from verbs, denoting verbal action or an instance of it; or denoting a substance involved in the verbal action
y:
From Proto-West Germanic *-ungu, from Proto-Germanic *-ungō.
Cognate with Old Saxon -unga (Low German -inge, -ing), Old Dutch -inga, -unga (Dutch -ing), Old High German -unga (German -ung), Old Norse -ung, -ing (Swedish -ing).

s: used to form adverbs from nouns, originally from verbal nouns
by halves, partially, to some extent, imperfectly
used to form adverbs from adjectives
used to create adverbs from pronouns
used to create adverbs from prepositions

s: suffix denoting inhabitants or residents of a place
the people of a city, the entire citizenry
suffix denoting inhabitants or residents of a place
residents of a burg, burghers, citizens
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-wari, from Proto-Germanic *warjaz (“dwellers of”). Cognate with Old High German -āri (“inhabitants of”).

s: Forming adjectives and nouns from adjectives or prepositions, with the sense of "in the direction of, toward".
Forming adverbs from adjectives or prepositions, with the sense of "in the direction of, toward".
y:
From Proto-Germanic *wardaz (“turned toward, in the direction of, facing”), from Proto-Indo-European *wert- (“to turn, wind”), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to turn, bend”).
Akin to Old Frisian -ward, Old Saxon -ward, Old Norse verðr, German -wärts. Cognate with Old English weorþan (“to turn (into), become”).
From Proto-West Germanic *-wardas, equivalent to -weard + -es.

s: suffix meaning tending toward, promoting, or exemplified by; -ing, -able
y: From Proto-West Germanic *wandī, from Proto-Germanic *wandijaz (“turning, directed”).
From weorþ or Proto-West Germanic *-werþ.
Derived from Proto-West Germanic *wirþī, from Proto-Germanic *wirþijaz (“worthy, worth”).
From Proto-Germanic *-wiljaz. Cognate with Gothic -𐍅𐌹𐌻𐌾𐌹𐍃 (-wiljis). Equivalent to willa + -e.

s:
c. 893, King Alfred's Laws
Tīenwintre cniht mæġ bēon þīefþe ġewita.
A ten-year-old boy can be an accessory to a theft.

late 9th century, The Old English Martyrology
Sanctus Iūstus wæs eahtawintre þā hē martyrdōm þrōwode for Criste.
Saint Justus was eight years old when he became a martyr for Christ.

c. 1020, Wulfstan, King Cnut's second law code
Wē willaþ þæt ǣlċ mann ofer twelfwintre selle þone āþ þæt hē nylle þēof bēon ne þēofes ġewita.
We want everyone over twelve years old to give an oath that they will not be a thief or a thief's accomplice.

late 9th century, translation of Orosius’ History Against the Pagans
Dioclētiānus and Maximiānus bebudon ēhtnesse cristenra manna—Dioclētiānus ēastane and Maximiānus westane—and for þām bebode wurdon fela martyra on tīenwintrum fierste.
Diocletian and Maximian ordered the persecution of Christians—Diocletian from the east and Maximian from the west—and because of that order there were many martyrs in a ten-year period.
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-wintrī, from Proto-Germanic *-wintruz. Cognate with Old Norse -vetr and Gothic -𐍅𐌹𐌽𐍄𐍂𐌿𐍃 (-wintrus). Equivalent to winter + -e. Compare the German suffix -jährig, of similar form and meaning.

s: denoting a specified way, manner, condition, habit or direction
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-wīs, from Proto-Germanic *-wīsaz, related to Old English wīse (“wise, manner, direction”).

s: state of, manner of, condition; direction
in the manner or fashion of; in the direction of
hyse (“son, youth”) + -wīse → hysewīse (“like a young man”)
y: From wīse (“manner, way, condition, direction”).
From combining form of Old English wist (“being”). Akin to Old English wesan (“to be”).

s: Forming adjectives and nouns from adjectives, with the sense of "a kind of speech".
Wes ðū ðīnum yldrum ārfæst symle, fæġerwyrde
Be thou ever honourable to thine elders, fair in word
þæt gē ne bēon tō biterwyrde, ne bealufulle on mōde
That ye be not bitter in speech, nor baleful in spirit
y: Compound words from Proto-Germanic *wurdiją. More at word.

s: Forming nouns from nouns or adjectives, with the sense of "a kind of speech".
They ordered him to give that answer
Ðæt ic mǣge sum rust on weg adrīfan of mīnre tungan, ðæt ic mǣge becuman to brǣddran gewyrde
That I may drive away some rust from my tongue, so that I may attain more broader verbosity
y: Compound words from Proto-Germanic *wurdiją. More at word.

s: alternative form of -e (a-stem/ō-stem dative singular suffix)
alternative form of -e (ō-stem accusative/genitive singular suffix)
forming abstract nouns from verbs, adjectives or other nouns; generally causing mutation of root or preceding vowels

s: forming abstract nouns from verbs, adjectives or other nouns; generally causing mutation of root or preceding vowels
y: Inherited from Proto-West Germanic *-þu, from Proto-Germanic *-þuz, from Proto-Indo-European *-tus.

s: forming abstract nouns from verbs, adjectives or other nouns; generally causing mutation of root or preceding vowels
y: Inherited from Proto-West Germanic *-þi, from Proto-Germanic *-þiz, from Proto-Indo-European *-tis.

s: instrumental suffix creating neuter nouns from verbs
hafenian (“to hold, to grasp”) → hæf → heaþor (“restraint, confinement”)
suffix used to denote the agent or means by which an action is performed
y: From Proto-West Germanic *-þr, from Proto-Germanic *-þrą, from Proto-Indo-European *-trom.
